description: We are needing in Python, fastAPI backend, and a frontend
summary:
We built the Astronaut Health Monitor, a real-time crew health dashboard for flight surgeons. Simulated astronaut vitals (heart rate, SpO2, temperature, blood pressure, respiration) stream into a FastAPI backend. There, an alert engine checks every reading in two ways: against safety limits that change with activity (rest, sleep, exercise, EVA), and against each astronaut’s own learned baseline. The results show up as tiered alerts (info, warning, critical) on a live web dashboard and an Android app, with trend charts for each vital.
Most monitors use fixed thresholds, so they miss changes that are abnormal for one person but under a generic limit. They also flood operators with false alarms during normal activity like exercise. Our engine catches a resting heart rate that drifts from 70 to 95, and it stays quiet when 130 bpm is expected during exercise. Debouncing, escalation, de-duplication, and keeping faulty readings out of the baseline mean fewer, more trustworthy alerts.
This matters because alarm fatigue makes people ignore alarms. On long missions far from Earth, crews need early warnings they can trust. The data is simulated; the engine is unit-tested.
details:
The intended goal of this project is to assist the monitoring of astronauts in space by both ground crew, and other astronauts. The benefits is has is that all members of the mission have access to a single source of alerts that is both quick and reliable. Another benefit is that astronauts, owing to their newfound ability to bring cellular smart devices with them, are able to install a well-optimized and aesthetically elegant mobile application that contains much of the same information of the dashboard.

The project is composed of two halves, the backend and the frontend. The backend is powered by FastAPI and Jinja, and is written in Python. We have two frontends, a web dashboard and an alternate flutter mobile application. The web dashboard is written in HTML+CSS+JS with HTMX and the mobile app in Dart.

We chose a rather simple frontend stack because often times modern frameworks bring a lot of bloat and complexity, of which can be a hindrance if the goal is to get quick and reliable alerts. Furthermore, simple tech stacks allow beginner developers to contribute to the project, reducing the surface area of poor quality code to surface. Likewise, since our project is reliant on a strong backend, we chose the battle-tested middleware library FastAPI, combined with HTMX and the Jinja2 templating language to to stream HTML fragments from the backend to the web dashboard. Alternatively, since much of our data is accessible through a REST API, other teams can quickly make ad-hoc frontends, and we were able to prototype a mobile application using Flutter -- and we were able to port all of its functions too!

We chose Flutter because of its cross-platform goal, and also because of its quick learning time. Thus giving us the ability, if we wanted to, to build for the Web, Android, iOS, Linux, MacOS, and Windows.

The SI agent we used is interchangeable with other agents, so long as the implementation we received from it exposes the same api route expected by the frontend.

We used primarily Windows and Linux powered hardware, but because we did not have a Mac device, we were only able to build the flutter mobile application for Android. If we had a Mac device, we also would have considered building for iOS.

We ultimately chose this project because much of the implementation work needed here landed much to our individual strengths and experience, and so we felt that this challenge was a less stressful way for us to build upon our knowledge.

We had to refactor and consider our architecture multiple times before we settled on what we finished with, in an attempt to make the project scalable and API coherent in the future.
dataRefs: NASA Spaceflight Human-System Standard Volume 1, Crew Health
